name: Therapeutic touch

card.summary: A hands-near-the-body healing practice from nursing that practitioners use for relaxation, pain relief and wound comfort, which people link to calmer, better-rested and better-healing skin and a more relaxed look.
card.aka: TT; non-contact therapeutic touch (NCTT); biofield therapy
card.note: Researchers report no detectable energy field; used as a complement, not a substitute for medical care.

quick.overview:
Therapeutic touch is a practice in which a practitioner holds their hands a few inches above, or lightly on, a clothed person's body and moves them in sweeping passes, aiming to sense and smooth a supposed human energy field. It was created in the early 1970s by nursing professor Dolores Krieger and the Theosophist Dora Kunz.

People interested in appearance come to it through the relaxation chain: calmer nerves, better sleep, less pain and tension, and support for wound healing, which in turn show up in the face and skin. Randomized trials have studied anxiety, pain, sleep and fatigue; the proposed energy field itself has been tested and not detected.
quick.how: A session usually lasts 10 to 20 minutes with the person seated or lying down, clothed. The practitioner centres themselves, passes their hands over the body to assess the field, smooths areas they perceive as disturbed, and then finishes. It is typically offered in hospitals, nursing settings and holistic clinics alongside conventional care, and people who use it for relaxation often report feeling calmer within a single session.
quick.risks: Direct physical harm is rarely reported, since there is usually no contact. The concern raised by clinicians and the American Cancer Society is that it could displace effective treatment for disease; it is described as a complement. Its core claim of a manipulable energy field has not been supported by controlled testing.

lead: Therapeutic touch (TT) is a complementary healing practice in which a practitioner moves their hands near, and sometimes on, a person's body to sense and rebalance what they describe as a human energy field. It was developed in the early 1970s by Dolores Krieger, a New York University nursing professor, together with Dora Kunz, a Theosophy figure who served as president of the Theosophical Society in America from 1975 to 1987 [1][16][18].

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles it is discussed through an indirect chain: relaxation, lower stress, better sleep and less pain lead to a calmer demeanour, healthier-looking skin and better recovery, while practitioners also claim it supports wound healing and so the way scars and skin recover. Nothing in the practice is a direct cosmetic treatment, and practitioners present it as a comfort and relaxation practice used alongside conventional care [2][16].

Research on TT is divided. Small clinical trials have looked at anxiety, pain, sleep and agitation, and some nursing reviews describe the findings as promising [2][8]. Studies of the underlying claim have not found a detectable field: in a 1998 JAMA experiment designed by nine-year-old Emily Rosa, 21 practitioners identified the position of her hand behind a screen 44% of the time [9][16][17]. Skeptical organisations and many reviewers regard the proposed mechanism as lacking plausibility, while nursing authors and practitioners continue to study and teach it as a supportive therapy [2][16].

chain: Hands passed near the body in a 10-20 minute session
Reported relaxation, less pain and tension, better sleep
Calmer, better-rested appearance and support for recovery
angle.text: People use TT as a relaxation and comfort practice, and the appearance payoff they describe comes from stress reduction and rest rather than from any change to the skin itself. Some practitioners also claim it supports wound healing, which would matter for how scars and skin recover.

paras: TT rests on the idea that people have an energy field that surrounds and interpenetrates the body, and that illness or distress corresponds to imbalance in it. Practitioners say they can feel warmth, tingling or pressure differences with their hands and can then smooth or redirect the field to restore balance [1][16].

Krieger described it as a contemporary form of laying-on-of-hands healing, but said it is unconnected to religion or faith healing [16]. A variant without any touching is called non-contact therapeutic touch (NCTT) [16][7]. In Canada, 'Therapeutic Touch' is a registered trademark for a practice in which no touching is required [16]. Proponents have drawn on Martha Rogers' nursing theory of unitary human beings and on interpretations of modern physics as theoretical support; a 2002 review by O'Mathuna and colleagues examined these justifications and found neither tenable [16].

The person remains fully clothed, seated or lying down, and a session commonly runs 10 to 20 minutes. Quackwatch's account lists four phases: centering, assessment, smoothing or 'unruffling' the field, and energy transfer [1][19]. The practitioner centres themselves, moves their hands a few inches above the body to assess the field, makes smoothing passes over areas of perceived disturbance, and closes the session [1].

Krieger began experiments with Kunz around 1971 and taught the method to her graduate nursing students at NYU, publishing a description in the American Journal of Nursing in 1975 [1]. Kunz, born in 1904 in the Dutch East Indies, was raised in the Theosophical movement and was a leader of the Theosophical Society in America; she said she could perceive auras, and her collaboration with Krieger is dated to 1972 in her biography [18]. Krieger presented the method as rooted in ancient laying-on-of-hands traditions and, per Kunz's account, in pranic healing [16][18].

The practice spread through nursing workshops and holistic-health networks. The professional body now known as Therapeutic Touch International Association was incorporated in 1979 as Nurse Healers-Professional Associates International, according to one encyclopedia account [1]. Physicist Alan Sokal reported in 2006 that over 80 colleges and universities in about 70 countries teach it and that about 80 hospitals in North America use it, while cautioning that advocates and critics may both exaggerate these figures. California's Board of Registered Nursing has accepted TT courses for continuing-education credit; skeptic groups presented the board with evidence against TT in 2006 and the policy did not change [16].

TT belongs to a family of energy or biofield therapies that includes Reiki, Healing Touch and Qigong [20][21]. Reiki, developed by Mikao Usui in Japan in the 1920s and brought to the United States by Hawayo Takata, differs mainly in that practitioners place their hands on the body, and a 2014 press report counted at least 60 US hospitals offering it [20]. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health separates 'veritable' energy medicine (measurable energies such as light or magnets) from 'putative' energy medicine (biofield healing), which it describes as based on energies that cannot be measured [21].

TT is not a cosmetic procedure. Its place in appearance culture comes from three claimed effects: stress and anxiety reduction, better sleep, and support for wound healing. Stress and poor sleep are commonly linked by users to dull skin, tension in the face and fatigue, so interventions that promote relaxation are discussed as supporting the look of the face. Randomized trials have studied TT for sleep quality and fatigue in menopausal women and for labor pain, and earlier trials examined anxiety in hospitalized patients and pain in burn patients [10][11][14][15].

A 1981 trial reported lower anxiety in hospitalized patients after TT [15], a 1986 study examined tension headache pain [13], and a 1998 study looked at pain and anxiety in burn patients [14]. A 1994 randomized crossover design tested non-contact TT with Reiki and other modalities on healing of full-thickness dermal wounds [7]. A small 1995 nursing pilot study measured physical signs and health perception after TT [22].

Nursing-literature reviews describe such studies as suggesting benefit for anxiety, relaxation, pain and wound healing, while noting research is at an early stage [2]. A best-evidence synthesis of biofield therapies assessed the research as a whole [8], and a 2000 systematic review of distant-healing trials examined the evidence for TT among other forms [12]. A scoping review of chemotherapy-induced neuropathy listed therapeutic touch among manipulative therapies that were studied and may be effective options [4]. Recent randomized trials have tested TT against distraction for labor pain and for sleep and fatigue in menopausal women [10][11].

The wound-healing and energy-field claims were also reviewed outside the nursing literature. A 2004 Cochrane review found no robust evidence that TT promotes healing of acute wounds, and was withdrawn in 2016 by its authors over concerns about the validity of included studies [16]. Reviewers including O'Mathuna and colleagues argue that, because the proposed mechanism has very low prior plausibility, methodological flaws are a likelier explanation for positive trials than a real effect; they and others also report that some positive findings were not replicated and note concern about publication bias [16]. Contextual factors such as the therapeutic ritual and practitioner touch are known to drive placebo responses in pain, which researchers cite when interpreting these trials [3]. Supporters respond that relaxation and comfort effects are worth studying in their own right [2].

Emily Rosa, born in 1987 in Loveland, Colorado, designed a single-blind test for a fourth-grade science fair. Practitioners placed their hands through holes in a cardboard screen while she hovered her hand, chosen by coin flip, over one of them; they tried to say which hand [17]. Fifteen practitioners were tested in 1996 and 13 in 1997 (seven of them repeats), 21 people in all [17]. They were correct in 122 of 280 trials, 44%, which is within the range expected by chance [9][19].

The paper, 'A Close Look at Therapeutic Touch', appeared in JAMA on 1 April 1998 with her mother Linda Rosa as lead author and Quackwatch's Stephen Barrett as senior author, making Emily the youngest author of a peer-reviewed medical paper (Guinness World Records recognised this in 1999) [9][17]. JAMA editor George Lundberg urged payers and patients to question funding for the practice absent experiments showing an effect [16]. The study drew international coverage, including a comparison in The New York Times to the child in The Emperor's New Clothes, and in 1998 Rosa keynoted the Ig Nobel ceremonies at Harvard and accepted an award on Krieger's behalf, as Krieger did not attend [17].

Critics of the study, among them David Hufford, questioned its ethics and framing as a school project [17]. A later study cited in coverage of the episode suggested people can detect a hand's radiant heat, and that blocking the heat reduced accuracy to chance [17]. The James Randi Educational Foundation separately offered a prize, eventually $1 million, for demonstrating detection of a human energy field under test conditions; per Quackwatch only one person attempted it and she did not succeed [19]. The American Cancer Society states that available evidence does not support claims that TT can cure cancer or other diseases [16].

TT is generally reported as safe with few adverse events, because it involves no or minimal contact [1]. The concerns that clinicians and organisations raise are indirect: that people may delay or replace effective treatment, and that resources may go to approaches whose proposed mechanism has not been demonstrated [1][16][20]. Reviewers of energy medicine in general link reliance on it in place of medical care to serious harm in some cases [21].

Coverage has mostly followed the Rosa study and its aftermath, in news reports, television programmes such as Scientific American Frontiers (which filmed the second round of testing) and skeptic-oriented shows [17]. Skeptical authors including Simon Singh and Edzard Ernst concluded in Trick or Treatment (2008) that the energy field was probably imaginary [16]. Nursing writers, by contrast, describe energy-based modalities as a growing area for supportive care and call for further research [2]. The debate has centred on whether nursing education and hospital practice should include a technique whose mechanism has not been shown by controlled tests [16].

timeline.event: Dora Kunz is born on Java; she later becomes a Theosophical Society leader [18].
Krieger and Kunz begin early experiments with healing touch [1].
Krieger and Kunz co-develop therapeutic touch, per Kunz's biography [18].
Krieger publishes a description of TT in the American Journal of Nursing [1].
Kunz serves as president of the Theosophical Society in America [16][18].
The TT professional association is incorporated as Nurse Healers-Professional Associates International [1].
A Nursing Research trial reports lower anxiety in hospitalized patients after TT [15].
Emily Rosa tests 21 practitioners in two rounds [17].
Rosa's experiment is published in JAMA on 1 April [9][17].
A systematic review of distant-healing trials, including TT, appears in Annals of Internal Medicine [12].
A Cochrane review finds no robust evidence for TT in acute wound healing; withdrawn in 2016 [16].
Alan Sokal reports TT is taught at over 80 colleges in about 70 countries and used in about 80 North American hospitals [16].
A randomized trial examines TT for sleep and fatigue in menopausal women [11].

lore.intro: Therapeutic touch is rarely discussed on appearance forums directly; it enters through wellness and relaxation talk. The claims below are those made by practitioners and by their critics in nursing and skeptic literature [1][16].

claims.claim: Practitioners can sense and manipulate a human energy field
claims.believers: Practitioners say they feel warmth, tingling or pressure differences near the body and use smoothing passes to rebalance the field [1][16].
claims.experts: In the Rosa study, 21 practitioners identified her hand 44% of the time, within the range expected by chance; the JAMA authors concluded the claim lacked a basis [9][19].

claims.claim: TT reduces anxiety, which shows in a calmer, better-rested look
claims.believers: Nursing authors report that studies suggest benefit for anxiety, relaxation and sense of well-being [2][15].
claims.experts: Reviewers say trials are small, methodologically limited and open to placebo and context effects; one review calls findings 'quite promising' but only suggestive [2][3][16].

claims.claim: TT speeds wound healing and so helps scars and skin recover
claims.believers: Practitioners cite studies of dermal-wound healing and describe wound recovery as a benefit [2][7].
claims.experts: A 2004 Cochrane review found no robust evidence for acute wounds and was withdrawn in 2016 over concerns about included studies [16].

claims.claim: TT eases pain, including headache, burn and labor pain
claims.believers: Trials in tension headache, burn patients and labor are cited as showing reduced pain [10][13][14].
claims.experts: Reviews attribute pain relief in such trials partly to contextual factors such as ritual and touch [3]; a distant-healing review found methodological limits [12].

claims.believers: A 2024 randomized trial in menopausal women tested TT for sleep quality and fatigue [11].
claims.experts: Single trials do not settle the question; reviewers say positive studies of low-plausibility therapies need replication [16].

claims.claim: It is a safe complement that can be used alongside normal care
claims.believers: Practitioners describe it as a supportive therapy used with, not instead of, conventional treatment [1][2].
claims.experts: Reports describe direct harm as rare; the American Cancer Society and others caution that it should not replace effective treatment [1][16].

claims.claim: TT is a form of or related to Reiki and other energy medicine
claims.believers: Energy-therapy teachers group TT, Healing Touch and Reiki as related energy-based modalities [2][20].
claims.experts: The NCCIH classes biofield healing as 'putative' energy medicine involving energies that cannot be verified [21].
